finding: The stdlib ledger writer still writes free text that PyYAML misreads or cannot parse. dispatch runs through uv run --script without PyYAML, so _scalar writes every ledger, and the reason of mark-blocked --reason is free text from the operator. _scalar quotes a string only when the stdlib loader would read it differently, and since this story also when it holds ": " or ends with ":". The review wrote 61 strings with _stdlib_dump and read them back. The stdlib loader returned every string unchanged. PyYAML failed or changed 37 of them, for example: "[WIP] waits on ST-0418" gives ParserError; "- see the CI log", "`uv sync` fails", "*.lock conflict" and "@reviewer asked" give ScannerError or ComposerError; "no" and "on" become booleans; "2026-11-19" becomes a date; "1:30" becomes 90. So any tool or test that loads a ledger with PyYAML, as the ST-0418 review did, fails or reads a wrong value. The fix of this story covers the records that dispatch writes itself, and those round-trip. The gap for free text looks unintended. The smallest fix is in _scalar: write a string plain only when it matches a conservative pattern, for example ^[A-Za-z0-9_./][A-Za-z0-9 _./,;()+-]*$, and is not a YAML 1.1 keyword such as yes, no, on, off, true, null, or a number or date form; quote every other string with json.dumps. Add a test that writes such strings with yaml set to None and reads them with yaml.safe_load.
why_this_severity: dispatch reads every ledger with its own stdlib loader, which returns each probed string unchanged, and every record that dispatch writes now round-trips through PyYAML (no to fails_purpose). A test, a review probe, or a python3 run with PyYAML installed fails on a ledger that holds such a reason, and the operator must find and quote the value by hand. The quoting rule exists unchanged in the installed copy, so in_use is true, but no installed tool reads a ledger with PyYAML, so harms_downstream is false.
